title: New monastics
hook: people living near the poor with daily prayer and shared meals

segments.voice: Yesterday, Iona: worship and the work of justice kept in one rule. Your line was prayer and politics. Which story did you read slowly? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-nine.

A row house on a block where cars rarely slow down. Inside, a handful of people share a kitchen, a budget and a prayer schedule. Before work, they pray around the table. In the evening the door is open, and a neighbor wanders in for soup and stays to talk. Nobody wears a habit. Nobody lives behind a wall. But they keep a rule, pray at set hours, share what they have, and they chose to live on this block on purpose, close to people who are struggling. Some people call them new monastics. Today: new monastics.

This block of the path has spent days with the old monastic families: Benedict's rule, the hours, the shared work. New monastics take that shape, a rule, set times of prayer, a common table, and plant it in ordinary neighborhoods instead of behind a cloister wall. They point back to the church's first days in Acts: "And all that believed were together, and had all things common." Two chapters later Luke says it again: they "were of one heart and of one soul," and none of them called what he had his own. A shared purse and a shared table sit close to the center of it. The other text they lean on is older. When the people of Judah were carried off to Babylon, the prophet Jeremiah sent them a letter. Other prophets were promising a quick return. Jeremiah wrote: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them." And then: "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." The Hebrew word for peace there is shalom: wholeness, well-being. Settle in. Pray for the place. Your good is tied up with its good. Christians talk about the label in different ways. For some monks and nuns, monastic means vows and a monastery, and they'd keep the word for that. New monastics say they're borrowing old wisdom, not replacing it, and some keep close friendships with monasteries. Either way, the picture is plain: prayer, a table, and neighbors who come to dinner.
screen: `A RULE, THE HOURS, A SHARED TABLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a meal with a neighbor. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people who live around you: next door, across the hall, down the street. Let one of them come forward. Now set a simple table in your mind. What would you serve? Soup, bread, takeout on paper plates. Where would you sit? When could it happen? If you pray, you can pray for that neighbor by name, and for the peace of your street. The bell holds the time.
New monastics. Christians who keep a rule of daily prayer and shared meals in ordinary neighborhoods, often near people who are struggling.
Your line: monks among us. Today, invite the neighbor you thought of: a meal, a coffee, a bowl of soup on the steps. Set a day. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: New monastic communities share a house or live near one another in struggling neighborhoods, keep a common rule with morning and evening prayer, share meals and resources, and open their tables to neighbors; members come from Protestant, Catholic and other churches.

notes: The hook is a composite scene; no particular community is named. Confirm it fairly pictures new monastic life.
'For some monks and nuns, monastic means vows and a monastery' is a general description; confirm. 'Some keep close friendships with monasteries' is also general.
'They often point back to Acts' and 'the other text they lean on' (Jeremiah 29) describe new monastic writing in general; confirm.
'They wanted to hear they'd be home soon' paraphrases the setting (Jeremiah 28–29, the false promise of a quick return); confirm.
